bridges.mechanism: A fall in global diesel supply reduces available bunker and marine diesel for sustained PLA sorties and patrols, directly cutting the tempo and duration of naval and air shows of force around Taiwan (and conversely a supply increase enables higher sortie rates).

Loss of Russian diesel exports forces importers to source refined product from more distant suppliers (Middle East, East Asia), directly increasing the volume of tanker shipments transiting routes and chokepoints used by Iran-Houthi-affected maritime traffic.

Diesel-driven disruptions to inland trucking, container drayage and short-sea shipping delay delivery of GPU/server hardware and spare parts, immediately reducing allocable compute in affected regions.

Sharp diesel price increases raise logistics and manufacturing costs across East Asian supply chains, worsening near‑term earnings outlooks and volatility for firms exposed to cross‑strait trade and thereby increasing the investor risk premium on assets linked to Taiwan/China.

A sustained rise in diesel prices raises near‑term inflation and fiscal outlays (via subsidies or weaker growth), deteriorating sovereign fiscal metrics and prompting investors to demand higher risk premia on eurozone sovereign debt.

Higher diesel prices raise the value of liquid cargoes and the economic payoff from interdiction or seizure, provoking insurers and charterers to demand larger risk premia for tankers operating in corridors vulnerable to Houthi action.

Large refinery outages disrupt fuel supplies to transport, logistics and industry, producing cash‑flow shocks and higher default rates among corporate borrowers concentrated in affected sectors, which in turn increases nonperforming loans and funding pressure in eurozone banks.

Higher sanctions‑evasion success demonstrated in the Russia–Ukraine context reveals practical procurement routes, intermediary networks and component substitution techniques that China can adopt or replicate to accelerate acquisition and integration of restricted technologies, raising its defense build rate.

An uptick in sanctions‑evasion activity raises compliance and counterparty risk for correspondent banks and asset managers, causing them to curtail or reroute eurozone inbound and outbound capital flows to avoid exposure or fines.

An observable rise in sanctions-evasion techniques linked to the Russia-Ukraine conflict incentivizes governments and coalitions to broaden and tighten enforcement and sanction regimes (including maritime measures) against networks perceived to use similar evasion channels involving Iran/Houthi-associated actors.

Larger government-held fuel reserves reduce the need for emergency seaborne imports through high-risk routes, lowering insurers' exposure and thereby reducing the shipping risk premium for tankers operating in Iran-Houthi-affected waterways.

A sudden surge in global demand for high‑end compute leads investors and funds to shift liquidity into hardware vendors, cloud issuances and technology financings, reducing the depth of orders and bid aggressiveness at eurozone sovereign auctions.

Rapid improvements in tactical and decision-support AI shorten sensor-to-shooter cycles and reduce manpower/risk for maritime and air probing operations, lowering the operational cost of conducting complex gray-zone coercive maneuvers and thus increasing their frequency/intensity.

Sharp, visible advances in AI capabilities drive large new equity and private capital rounds concentrated in US/China tech firms, prompting portfolio managers and allocators to pull capital out of European bond and equity markets and send net flows toward those tech hubs.

Improved model capabilities produce higher-quality synthetic documents, forged paperwork, multilingual social-engineering and routing optimizers that directly enable actors to create plausible cover paperwork and operationalize alternative trade channels to evade sanctions.

An uptick in AI-driven safety failures (false targeting, fratricide, autonomous platform losses) among deployed systems increases caution and tighter rules of engagement for forces operating in the Taiwan theater, reducing the frequency and aggressiveness of gray-zone coercive actions.

A rise in cyber operations targeting AI models, cloud infrastructure, and maritime/air C2 pushes military planners to accelerate procurement, hardening, and redundant integration of defense systems, raising the pace of capability build-out.

Increased hostile cyber operations tied to US–China rivalry that target European financial infrastructure cause outages, fraud losses and confidence shocks that strain bank liquidity, trigger higher funding costs and raise solvency concerns.

An uptick in cyber operations tied to US–China AI competition spills into maritime cyber effects (AIS/GPS spoofing, port IT compromises) in the Red Sea/Gulf area, producing operational disruptions and losses that drive insurers and charterers to demand higher risk premia for fuel shipments.

A rise in targeted cyber operations against industrial control systems and IT at refineries and terminals can directly force units offline and reduce throughput by causing shutdowns, safety trips, or persistent operational disruption.

Escalated cyberattacks on ports, fuel terminals, pipeline control systems or shipping logistics systems can directly halt or delay deliveries and exports, reducing the net flow of diesel into commercial markets.

A drop in tanker transit from Houthi attacks or interdiction produces immediate energy import shortfalls and higher import bills for euro-area importers, prompting foreign investors to reduce exposures to affected sovereign and corporate assets and causing net capital outflows from the Eurozone.

A fall in tanker transit volumes through Red Sea/Bab el-Mandeb chokepoints directly reduces deliveries of refined diesel and crude feedstocks from Middle Eastern exporters to global markets, lowering net diesel inflows.

Higher maritime shipping risk premiums immediately raise costs, margins uncertainty and insurance exposure for firms trading across the Taiwan Strait and regional supply chains, causing investors to demand higher risk premia on China- and Taiwan-exposed assets.

A rise in the shipping risk premium increases uncertainty in oil, freight and insurance costs, triggering rapid repricing of energy-linked instruments and derivatives and driving up realized and implied volatility across European fixed‑income and related markets.
Rising insurance, war-risk and freight premia for tanker voyages are passed into delivered fuel costs, quickly lifting benchmark diesel prices across major trading hubs.

Rising shipping insurance premiums signal escalating maritime confrontation and incentivize state and proxy actors to launch cyber operations against adversary logistics, port, and cloud infrastructures (including AI toolchains) to exploit or exacerbate supply‑chain stress.

Repeated upstream production shut‑ins increase energy-price volatility and highlight import vulnerability, prompting Chinese authorities to accelerate procurement and force-projection investments (naval logistics, escorts, stockpiles) to secure sea lines of supply.
Sustained upstream production shut‑ins reduce available crude feedstock for regional refineries, forcing lower runs or temporary idling and thus reducing operational throughput.

Escalatory sanctions targeting maritime actors provoke retaliatory or preemptive disruptive maritime behavior and divert US/allied attention and assets, creating an operational window that China can exploit to increase gray‑zone coercive pressure on Taiwan.

Escalation of sanctions or aggressive policy measures tied to Iran/Houthi maritime incidents raises compliance and trade frictions for European firms and increases near‑term fiscal uncertainty (through higher subsidies, energy costs or trade disruption), leading investors to demand wider sovereign credit spreads for affected euro-area issuers.

Escalation of targeted sanctions and enforcement against Iran/Houthi shipping incentivizes the expansion and refinement of concealment tactics (e.g., ship‑to‑ship transfers, opaque flags, broker networks) that increase the global rate at which sanctioned flows are routed around restrictions and can be adopted by other sanctioned actors.

Greater maritime-focused sanctions and secondary‑sanctions enforcement (inspections, port denials, carrier blacklisting) directly block or delay shipments of semiconductor fabrication equipment, test gear and datacenter hardware into China, reducing immediately allocable compute hardware capacity.

Rising eurozone sovereign spreads raise government borrowing costs and fiscal pressure, prompting postponement of planned purchases or refilling of national strategic fuel stocks and/or sales of reserve inventories to cover budgets, thereby lowering reserve levels.

A sustained rise in sovereign credit spreads raises borrowing costs and valuation pressure for European carriers and data‑centre operators, prompting capex delays or cancellations that reduce available installed/allocable compute capacity accessible to global AI workloads.

Spikes in eurozone market volatility increase global hedge and margin costs and push up cross‑asset implied volatilities, which lifts the cost of insuring and holding assets linked to Taiwan and therefore raises the investor risk premium on those exposures.

Spikes in eurozone-driven financial market volatility raise cross‑asset risk premia and push insurers, owners and charterers to reprice hazard exposure for Red Sea/GoG transits, lifting the shipping risk premium demanded on tankers.

Increased eurozone fixed‑income and related market volatility raises risk premia and drives short‑term flows into commodity futures and physical commodity hoarding, pushing up diesel spot and futures prices across major hubs.

Acute stress in eurozone banks contracts trade‑finance, reduces availability of letters of credit and counterparty capacity to back marine insurance/reinsurance, and thus forces insurers and charterers to charge higher premiums for tanker voyages through Houthi‑exposed routes.

Heightened bank stress leads banks to curtail trade finance, letters of credit and correspondent services used to finance and insure cross‑border fuel shipments, directly reducing the volume of diesel imports/exports that can be executed.

When eurozone banking stress tightens lending to technology firms, many firms accelerate migration of AI training and inferencing to large US or Chinese cloud providers, increasing compute consumption intensity on those providers and concentrating demand in the US–China rivalry.

An abrupt net outflow of capital from eurozone sovereign and credit markets triggers global portfolio rebalancing and liquidity withdrawal from Asia, reducing demand for Taiwan‑exposed assets and raising the risk premium investors require to hold them.

Higher net cross‑border capital flows through eurozone channels increase the availability of financing for shipping, insurance and opaque intermediary firms that facilitate rerouting/payments around sanctions, raising the rate of sanctions evasion.

An increase in net cross‑border capital into eurozone sovereign/credit markets diverts institutional capital away from data‑centre and hyperscaler expansion elsewhere, reducing the pace of compute capacity buildouts in US/China, whereas a decline in those flows tends to redirect investment toward US/Chinese cloud expansion.

Acute spikes in coercive military actions around Taiwan trigger immediate global risk repricing and surge in hedging activity, raising realized and implied volatility in eurozone fixed‑income and related derivatives markets.
Escalation in gray‑zone coercion prompts a flight‑to‑quality that reallocates international portfolio flows into core eurozone sovereign bonds, increasing net inflows into euro area markets.

A spike in gray‑zone coercion around Taiwan forces redistribution of US/allied naval assets and raises insurer perceptions of correlated naval risk, prompting shipowners and insurers to reprice Middle East fuel routes and raise shipping premiums.

Sustained increases in coercive incidents drive shipping firms to avoid transits through chokepoints perceived as underprotected (e.g., Red Sea/Suez) because of reduced escort availability and tighter ROE, reducing tanker voyage frequency through those corridors.

Escalation of harassment and near‑shore military activity in the Taiwan Strait forces rerouting and delays for tankers and refined‑product shipments through key Asia hubs (Strait of Malacca/Singapore), raising freight and short‑term diesel scarcity that pushes up global diesel prices.

Sustained gray‑zone coercion prompts US and allied defense and intelligence agencies to accelerate development and deployment of AI-enabled ISR, targeting, and wargaming models, increasing demand for high‑performance training and inference compute.

Escalating maritime and air coercion triggers complementary hybrid operations (including offensive cyber and espionage) aimed at disrupting adversary command, AI data pipelines, and supporting infrastructure, raising the tempo of malicious cyber activity.

A rapid defense procurement and production push reallocates semiconductors, accelerators, and manufacturing capacity toward military systems and prompts export controls/prioritization, reducing the compute capacity available for civilian and commercial AI use (especially to rival actors).

A rise in the geopolitical investor risk premium raises required yields for exposed assets and reduces investor willingness to place competitive bids, lowering order volumes and bid‑to‑cover ratios at eurozone debt auctions.

Rising investor risk premia tied to China‑Taiwan tensions contract capital and reinsurance capacity available to shipping firms, increasing financing and insurance costs which are passed through as higher shipping risk premiums for fuel transport in the Gulf/Red Sea.

Rising geopolitical risk premia make investors less willing to fund long‑horizon, capital‑intensive AI model development in exposed firms and jurisdictions, slowing project scale‑ups and therefore the pace of model capability improvement.

nodes.label: Sanctions enforcement strength

nodes.label: Sanctions evasion rate

nodes.label: Military strike rate

nodes.label: Critical infrastructure damage level
nodes.description: Aggregate functional loss across key infrastructure types (transport nodes, power, refineries, data centres) relative to baseline.

nodes.label: Intelligence-sharing level
nodes.description: Extent and reliability of operational intelligence exchange between aligned actors measured by volume and timeliness.

nodes.label: Diplomatic trust index
nodes.description: Mutual confidence between external actors in diplomatic and negotiation contexts measured by perceived reliability and cooperation willingness.

nodes.label: Domestic political pressure for energy action
nodes.description: Intensity of domestic political incentives and pressures pushing for immediate changes in energy supply or policy.

nodes.label: Fuel price expectations

nodes.label: Energy market liquidity
nodes.description: Depth and ease of trading in fuel markets measured by bid-ask spreads, volumes, and ability to transact large orders without price spikes.

nodes.label: Freight and shipping costs

nodes.label: Cyberattack frequency on infrastructure
nodes.description: Rate of cyber intrusions and disruptive operations targeting critical infrastructure per unit time.

nodes.label: Strategic fuel reserves level
nodes.description: Quantity of government or market-held fuel stocks available for emergency release measured as days of consumption.

Compute demand intensity
nodes.description: The rate at which organizations and models request and consume high-performance compute resources for AI workloads.

nodes.label: Compute supply capacity
nodes.description: The available installed and allocable compute resources (GPUs/accelerators, servers, cloud instances) that can be provisioned for AI tasks.

nodes.label: Model capability growth
nodes.description: The pace at which AI model performance, complexity, and functional capabilities advance over time.

nodes.label: Safety incident rate
nodes.description: The frequency at which deployed AI systems produce harmful, unsafe, or otherwise unintended outcomes requiring remediation.

nodes.label: Cyber attack activity
nodes.description: The intensity and frequency of malicious cyber operations targeting AI systems, infrastructure, or data.

nodes.label: Regulatory scrutiny level
nodes.description: The degree and strictness of oversight, rules, and investigatory attention directed at AI development and deployment.

nodes.label: Financing availability
nodes.description: The amount and ease of access to debt, equity, and other capital sources available to AI-related ventures and projects.

nodes.label: Investor confidence
nodes.description: The prevailing sentiment among investors regarding the risk/return prospects of AI-sector assets and financings.

nodes.label: Chip supply resilience
nodes.description: The ability of semiconductor production and distribution networks to absorb disruptions and meet AI chip demand.

nodes.label: Talent availability
nodes.description: The supply of individuals with relevant AI research, engineering, and operations skills available to organizations.

nodes.label: Data accessibility
nodes.description: The ease and legality with which training, fine-tuning, and operational data can be obtained and used by AI developers.

nodes.label: Legal liability exposure
nodes.description: The aggregate level of potential legal and litigation risk faced by actors deploying or commercializing AI systems.

nodes.label: Valuation volatility
nodes.description: The extent and rate of short-term fluctuations in market valuations and prices of AI-related assets and securities.

nodes.label: Enterprise adoption rate
nodes.description: The speed at which commercial organizations integrate AI systems into core business processes and products.

nodes.label: Public trust in technology
nodes.description: The level of societal confidence in technological systems and institutions to operate safely, fairly, and transparently.

nodes.label: Disclosure transparency
nodes.description: The typical openness and clarity with which organizations report performance, revenue, safety incidents, and security issues related to AI.

Global crude production rate
nodes.description: The aggregate volume of crude oil produced per unit time across upstream operations in the system.

nodes.label: Global refining throughput
nodes.description: The total volume of crude and intermediate fuels processed by refineries per unit time.

nodes.label: Seaborne tanker transit volume
nodes.description: The rate and volume of liquid hydrocarbon cargoes transiting maritime routes and chokepoints.

nodes.label: Shipping risk premium
nodes.description: The additional market price charged or demanded to compensate for perceived risk in maritime transport of fuels.

nodes.label: Maritime insurance premia level
nodes.description: The average cost level of insurance coverage for maritime energy shipments and vessels.

nodes.label: Strategic fuel inventory stocks
nodes.description: The aggregate volume of stored crude and refined fuels held in inventory across strategic and commercial reserves.

nodes.label: Refining capacity utilization
nodes.description: The proportion of installed refinery processing capacity that is actively in operation.

nodes.label: Logistics rerouting rate
nodes.description: The speed and frequency at which fuel supply chains change transport routes and modes in response to disruptions.

nodes.label: Airspace operational closure extent
nodes.description: The spatial and temporal extent of flight restrictions and airspace closures affecting aviation fuel demand and flows.

nodes.label: Storm intensity and frequency
nodes.description: The prevailing rate and severity of weather systems (storms, hurricanes) that impact production, transport and infrastructure.

nodes.label: Upstream production shut-in rate
nodes.description: The rate at which upstream oil and gas production is taken offline or curtailed due to operational or safety reasons.

nodes.label: Alternative route capacity
nodes.description: The available throughput capacity of non-primary transport routes and modalities that can substitute for disrupted links.

nodes.label: Market price volatility
nodes.description: The short-term variability and expected fluctuation amplitude in energy commodity prices.

nodes.label: Investor risk appetite for energy
nodes.description: The prevailing willingness of investors to allocate capital to energy-sector assets given perceived systemic risks.

nodes.label: Route concentration index
nodes.description: The degree to which energy trade flows are concentrated on a small number of routes or chokepoints.

nodes.label: Sanctions and policy response intensity
nodes.description: The level and aggressiveness of trade, financial and regulatory measures applied in response to geopolitical tensions affecting energy flows.

Global bond rout: rising sovereign yields and political-financial stress
Sovereign nominal yields
nodes.description: The prevailing nominal interest rates on sovereign debt across the sovereign bond market.

nodes.label: Sovereign real yields
nodes.description: Inflation-adjusted yields on sovereign debt that reflect the real return available to investors.

nodes.label: Yield curve slope
nodes.description: The difference between long-term and short-term sovereign yields indicating term premium and expectations.

nodes.label: Sovereign credit spreads
nodes.description: The premium demanded by investors for holding a given sovereign's debt relative to a baseline benchmark across maturities.

nodes.label: Government debt stock
nodes.description: The outstanding stock of government debt measured relative to the economy size and other scaling metrics.

nodes.label: Fiscal balance (flow)
nodes.description: The net government borrowing or surplus per period, measured as the fiscal deficit or surplus relative to economic output.

nodes.label: Government debt issuance rate
nodes.description: The volume and pacing of new government debt offered to markets per unit of time.

nodes.label: Auction demand
nodes.description: The aggregate level of investor orders and bidding pressure at sovereign debt issuances and auctions.

nodes.label: Bond market liquidity
nodes.description: The ease, depth, and cost of trading sovereign and credit bonds, including bid-ask spreads and market depth.

nodes.label: Market volatility
nodes.description: The degree of price variability and realized or implied volatility across fixed income and related asset markets.

nodes.label: Investor risk appetite
nodes.description: The prevailing willingness of market participants to hold risk assets versus seeking safe-haven instruments.

nodes.label: Investment-grade credit spreads
nodes.description: The yield premium on investment-grade corporate debt over comparable sovereign or benchmark yields.

nodes.label: High-yield credit spreads
nodes.description: The yield premium on lower‑rated corporate and speculative‑grade debt over comparable sovereign or benchmark yields.

nodes.label: Banking sector stress
nodes.description: The degree of funding, solvency and market‑value pressure across banks arising from asset‑liability mismatches and market moves.

nodes.label: Policy rate expectations
nodes.description: Market-implied expectations of future short-term policy interest rates and the path of monetary policy.

nodes.label: Cross-border capital flows
nodes.description: Net international flows of capital into and out of sovereign and credit markets measured per period.

European bank-stock selloff and funding stress

Military coercion intensity
nodes.description: The aggregate intensity of coercive military actions and shows of force across the contested maritime and airspace arena.

nodes.label: Gray-zone activity rate
nodes.description: The frequency and tempo of ambiguous, below-threshold operations (patrols, militia actions, symbolic provocations) in contested areas.

nodes.label: Diplomatic signaling rate
nodes.description: The cadence and intensity of formal and informal diplomatic messages, protests, and public positioning between rival actors and their partners.

nodes.label: Alliance commitment
nodes.description: The aggregate degree of stated and implicit security commitment among aligned actors toward mutual defense and cooperation.

nodes.label: Defense capability build rate
nodes.description: The pace at which military capabilities (procurement, production, training) are increased and modernized.

nodes.label: Defense budget share
nodes.description: The share of public fiscal resources allocated to defense and security relative to total public spending.

nodes.label: Investor risk premium
nodes.description: The additional cost investors demand to hold assets exposed to geopolitical tensions, reflected in pricing spreads and risk-adjusted returns.

nodes.label: Capital flow volatility
nodes.description: The short-term variability in cross-border capital movements and asset reallocations in response to geopolitical signals.

nodes.label: Trade and supply-chain exposure
nodes.description: The degree to which economies and firms depend on contested-region trade links, inputs, and production networks.

nodes.label: Domestic political polarization
nodes.description: The intensity of domestic political division over foreign and fiscal policy choices that shapes decision-making agility.

nodes.label: Fiscal policy flexibility
nodes.description: The available fiscal headroom and willingness to reallocate or increase public spending for defense, stimulus, or mitigation.

nodes.label: Public support for rearmament
nodes.description: The level of public approval for increased defense spending and militarized posture.

nodes.label: Regional integration cohesion
nodes.description: The strength of institutional and political cohesion among neighboring states for coordinated economic and security responses.

nodes.label: Regulatory and economic pressure
nodes.description: The intensity of non-military state tools (taxes, sanctions, regulatory actions, industrial policy) applied as strategic leverage.

nodes.label: Media and signal amplification rate
nodes.description: The speed and breadth with which incidents, narratives, and political signals are amplified through media and social channels.

nodes.label: Economic growth momentum
nodes.description: The underlying pace of economic activity and near-term growth expectations that condition policy choices and investor behavior.

An increase in net cross‑border capital into eurozone sovereign/credit markets diverts institutional capital away from data‑centre and hyperscaler expansion elsewhere, reducing the pace of compute capacity buildouts in US/China, whereas a decline in those flows tends to redirect investment toward US/Chinese cloud expansion.

Acute spikes in coercive military actions around Taiwan trigger immediate global risk repricing and surge in hedging activity, raising realized and implied volatility in eurozone fixed‑income and related derivatives markets.
Escalation in gray‑zone coercion prompts a flight‑to‑quality that reallocates international portfolio flows into core eurozone sovereign bonds, increasing net inflows into euro area markets.

A spike in gray‑zone coercion around Taiwan forces redistribution of US/allied naval assets and raises insurer perceptions of correlated naval risk, prompting shipowners and insurers to reprice Middle East fuel routes and raise shipping premiums.

Sustained increases in coercive incidents drive shipping firms to avoid transits through chokepoints perceived as underprotected (e.g., Red Sea/Suez) because of reduced escort availability and tighter ROE, reducing tanker voyage frequency through those corridors.

Escalation of harassment and near‑shore military activity in the Taiwan Strait forces rerouting and delays for tankers and refined‑product shipments through key Asia hubs (Strait of Malacca/Singapore), raising freight and short‑term diesel scarcity that pushes up global diesel prices.

Sustained gray‑zone coercion prompts US and allied defense and intelligence agencies to accelerate development and deployment of AI-enabled ISR, targeting, and wargaming models, increasing demand for high‑performance training and inference compute.

Escalating maritime and air coercion triggers complementary hybrid operations (including offensive cyber and espionage) aimed at disrupting adversary command, AI data pipelines, and supporting infrastructure, raising the tempo of malicious cyber activity.

A rapid defense procurement and production push reallocates semiconductors, accelerators, and manufacturing capacity toward military systems and prompts export controls/prioritization, reducing the compute capacity available for civilian and commercial AI use (especially to rival actors).

A rise in the geopolitical investor risk premium raises required yields for exposed assets and reduces investor willingness to place competitive bids, lowering order volumes and bid‑to‑cover ratios at eurozone debt auctions.

Rising investor risk premia tied to China‑Taiwan tensions contract capital and reinsurance capacity available to shipping firms, increasing financing and insurance costs which are passed through as higher shipping risk premiums for fuel transport in the Gulf/Red Sea.

Rising geopolitical risk premia make investors less willing to fund long‑horizon, capital‑intensive AI model development in exposed firms and jurisdictions, slowing project scale‑ups and therefore the pace of model capability improvement.
